case_name: Beaudoin v Agriculture Financial Services Corporation
text:
Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Beaudoin
v Agriculture Financial Services Corporation, 2018 ABQB 627

Date:
20180828

Docket:
1601 07189

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Sandra Beaudoin

Plaintiff

- and -

Agriculture Financial Services Corporation

Defendant

_______________________________________________________

Memorandum of Decision

of

A.R. Robertson
, Q.C., Master in Chambers

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

This is a wrongful dismissal claim in which just
cause is pled as a defence. The parties have agreed that it is an appropriate
case to be dealt with by way of summary judgment.

[
2
]

If the defence of just cause is not accepted,
then the parties agree that it is appropriate for the Court to decide the
consequential damage issues, being the “reasonable notice” period, whether the
plaintiff failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate her claim, and whether it
is an appropriate case to award punitive or aggravated damages, and if so, to
set the amount.

[
3
]

The parties provided the Court with a binder
entitled “Agreed Statement of Facts and Joint Documents”, reflecting the extent
to which the basic relevant facts are not in dispute.  I commend counsel for
their collaboration in preparing this binder.

[
4
]

In some cases an inference must be drawn from
the known facts.

[
5
]

I have concluded that there was not just cause
for dismissal and I award damages based on 14 months’ “reasonable notice”.

Background

[
6
]

Agriculture Financial Services Corporation
(“AFSC”) is a provincial Crown Corporation providing the agriculture industry
with loans, crop insurance, and farm income disaster assistance. Its head
office is in Lacombe, and it has 44 branch offices located across Alberta.  One
of them is in Hanna, where the plaintiff worked.

[
7
]

Ms. Beaudoin started work with AFSC in Hanna on
March 20, 2000.  She worked consistently, on a full-time basis, until she was
dismissed on November 30, 2015.

[
8
]

Ms. Beaudoin was initially employed as an
administrative support employee in the Crop Insurance Department, then in 2014
she was given the position of Product Specialist III Lending, Sales and Markets,
a position referred to as a “Lender”.  Her responsibilities included assessing
clients’ circumstances to determine fit and qualifications for loans, processing
and managing clients’ accounts, and developing and maintaining business
relationships with AFSC clients.

[
9
]

Ms. Beaudoin’s immediate superior was located in
Drumheller, and her superior in turn reported to Mr. Kelly Thompson, based in
Parkland.

The Factual Matrix Leading to
Dismissal

The First Sequence of Emails

[
10
]

On June 4, 2015, one of AFSC’s clients asked Ms.
Beaudoin whether she could provide the client with a written opinion regarding
the value of certain lands belonging to a company owned by the client’s
daughter and son-in-law. The daughter and son-in-law were going through a
divorce.  Ms. Beaudoin advised the client that she would ask her superiors.  She
did, by email of the same day, and the next morning her superior replied by
email, “We are not allowed to share our opinions on land values with outside
parties. This could have serious legal implications for us”.

[
11
]

Ms. Beaudoin replied to Ms. Wilkins by email,
“As I mentioned in my email I told the clients I would ask but was doubtful I
could give them anything.”

[
12
]

I note that the email sent by Ms. Beaudoin, and
all of the replies in the same email string, indicate as the subject, “Can my
opinion of Land Values be released to clients.”

[
13
]

She then sent an email to the client with the
subject “Land values”: “As I alluded to you yesterday in our conversation, we
use our land value determination for internal purposes only & cannot
provide written documentation regarding our opinions of land values for your
situation.”

[
14
]

A few minutes later, Ms. Beaudoin provided to
the son-in-law of the client, being the husband in the divorce proceedings, an
email providing him with loan balances of his farm corporation, and then
stated, in response to an earlier request by him,

We appraise land values for AFSC financing
purposes only & do not provide written documentation regarding our opinions
of land values.  If you want a land appraisal, I suggest you seek a land
appraiser to provide you with the information you are looking for.

The Second Sequence of Emails

[
15
]

A little over three months later, on August 11,
2015, she made a note to the AFSC file to the effect that the mother of the
divorcing woman, who had initially contacted her, brought in an affidavit
verifying corporate signing authority.  Her email went on to say this: said,

Gave her copies of the Asset Values of the
land for the loans approved previous to give her an idea of land values to
support her daughter’s divorce. Advised her that I’m not able to give her
current land value since we are not licensed appraisers. But she could have the
info of what their land was valued at when the increased the revolving loan
values June 2015.  Suggested she also try the MD of Acadia Valley as we get
info from them for comparable sales in the area & they may be able to help
her out.

[
16
]

An important detail is that she did not give
appraisal information to the client on her daughter and son-in-law’s farm
company’s land; she gave information to the client on her own land.  That is,
the information she provided was not in direct contradiction of the direction
she had been given in June.

Management Review of Emails

[
17
]

About three months afterwards, on November 10,
Ms. Beaudoin received an email from Mr. Thompson (her superior two steps above)
saying that in a review of her files and portfolio management the August 11 memo
to file had been discovered.  He asked two questions:

1.

Did you keep a photocopy of the affidavit and
scan it into Erma?  If so please email it to me.

2.

Which document specifically did you provide [the
customer] with when you speak to giving her copies of the Asset Values?

[
18
]

There was no mention made that Ms. Beaudoin’s
job was in jeopardy. The subject line of the email was, “Review”.

[
19
]

Ms. Beaudoin responded that she did not have a
copy of the affidavit as it was a legal document and would have been forwarded
to “AMS”, which I assume is a department of AFSC. She explained that the
documents she would have given to the customer, “would have been the appraisal
summary or the Present Security Position on Current Asset Values per attached.”

[
20
]

A few minutes later, she sent another email to
Mr. Thompson asking, “Is there a problem?”

[
21
]

A few minutes after that, she sent another email
to Mr. Thompson explaining the relationship between the customers involved.  She
then said,

Not sure if this is useful, but thought I
would share it with you.  She wanted to know what I would value her daughter’s
land at which I did not provide but as outlined below, gave her info on her own
land & gave her a suggestion where to find additional info. I did not give
her values of what [her daughter and son-in-law’s company’s] land would be.

Dismissal

[
22
]

Twenty days later, on November 30, 2015, Mr.
Thompson gave her a letter terminating her employment, signed by the Senior
Manager, Human Resources & Payroll.  The letter made reference to the AFSC
Code of Conduct and the Lending Policy Manual, “both of which prohibit the
supply of appraisals to clients.” It asserted that after being specifically
told that she could not supply “the foregoing appraisal report” she did so anyway.
The letter asserted that her behaviour constituted wilful disobedience and
insubordination and exposed the corporation to liability. The letter said, “We
have lost all trust in you and have no choice but to terminate your employment
for just cause.”

[
23
]

The letter advised Ms. Beaudoin that AFSC would
continue the Homewood Human Solutions EFAP coverage for two months. This would
give Ms. Beaudoin and her dependents access to up to 6 confidential one-on-one
sessions with a registered psychologist or counsellor. Confidentiality was
promised.

[
24
]

Ms. Beaudoin was then 54 years old.

[
25
]

As indicated in the emails, it is not clear
precisely what documents Ms. Beaudoin gave to the customer, because the
question was first asked of her over three months after she provided it.

AFSC’s Policies

[
26
]

AFSC’s Lending Policy Manual specifically says,
under the headings “Security – Valuation” and “Real Property”, that, “Appraisals
completed by AFSC staff must not be given to customers.”  It does not set out
any particular consequence if this direction is breached.

[
27
]

AFSC’s Code of Conduct and Ethics policy, made
effective February 1, 2015 specifically gave this direction, under the heading
“Protection of AFSC’s Properties and Information”, “You will protect the
properties and safeguard the confidentiality of all non-public information of AFSC,
its customers, employees and suppliers (past, present and prospective).”

[
28
]

However, that sentence immediately followed the
sentence, “Our relationships with customers, suppliers and with each other are
based on trust.”  Accordingly, in context the direction to protect
confidentiality seems focused on protecting relationships with “customers,
suppliers and with each other.”  Ms. Beaudoin’s position, discussed below, is
that her disclosure to a customer of the customer’s own dated land value was
done to protect the relationship.

[
29
]

Nonetheless, it went on to specifically provide,
as follows:

Any product or technology you develop in the
course of your duties with AFSC is the property of AFSC.  You shall not sell,
trade, market or distribute any such product or technology unless otherwise
authorized by the Administrator or Designate.

[
30
]

I note that this direction does not specifically
address sharing information with customers about their own loan data.  The
prohibition not to “distribute any such product” might be read as meaning that.

[
31
]

The Code of Conduct and Ethics policy addressed
the possible consequences of a breach generically:

If you do not comply with the standards of
behaviour identified in this Code, including taking part in a decision or
action that furthers your private interest, you may be subject to disciplinary
action up to and including termination of your employment….

[
32
]

However, the Code also specifically set out a
process that was supposed to be followed once a potential breach had been
reported.  It specifically provided that,

The accused employee… has the right to
complete information and the right to respond to the potential breach. The
identity of the reporter will not be disclosed unless required by law or in a
legal proceeding. The administrator will make a decision and complete a report
of the review in a timely manner. The decision may range from finding no
potential breach to one that reveals suspected criminal conduct.

[
33
]

This aspect of the Code was not properly
followed by AFSC management.  The HR manager and Mr. Thompson reviewed the June
4 and 5 emails and the November 10 emails and recommended to the president of
the Corporation, Brad Klak, that Ms. Beaudoin’s employment be terminated for
cause.

[
34
]

However, of significance is that Ms. Beaudoin
was not given an opportunity to respond to the “potential breach”.  Her first
ability to respond was in the context of this lawsuit.

Evidence Pertinent to Damages
Assessment

[
35
]

There is no evidence of the value of Ms.
Beaudoin’s benefits.  She did not take advantage of the Employee and Family
Assistance Plan mentioned in the termination letter.

[
36
]

Her annual base salary was $89,808.  She was 54
years old at the time of termination, and lived in Hanna, which is a small town
with a population of approximately 2,700.  She lives with her husband and
family, and has not started replacement employment.  She has searched for
replacement employment by reviewing the local newspaper and webpages.

[
37
]

Ms. Beaudoin graduated from the University of
Alberta in 1985 with a Bachelor of Science (Agriculture) degree.

[
38
]

After termination, she was, as she described it
in questioning, “offered a job with the Bank shortly after I was done, and I
declined because it was not in the state of mind to be working with the
public.”  That “offer” was possible employment with the Chinook Credit Union,
and the agriculture lender asked her if she would work with them.  That offer
came approximately two weeks to a month after termination.  It was a lending
position in the Hanna office of Chinook Credit Union, a position similar to her
former position at AFSC. She turned it down when it was presented, apparently
orally.  It does not appear to have ever been made formally.

Ms. Beaudoin’s Explanation

[
39
]

In Ms. Beaudoin’s affidavit she explained the
documents that she likely provided to the customer:

While I did not recall the exact
circumstances described in the [August 11] note, I surmised that back in August
I likely provided [the customer] with an Appraisal Summary or a Present
Security Position on the Current Asset Values form, neither of which contained
current information or disclose my opinion as to the value of the Lands.

[
40
]

She provided this explanation for why she did
this:

I take full responsibility for providing
land assessment information to [the customer].  It was my understanding at the
time, rightly or wrongly, that I was assisting a valuable client with a
difficult problem within the bounds of my professional mandate and AFSC’s
rules.

I did not intentionally disobey [my
supervisor].  I would never wilfully contravene a direct order from one of my
superiors.  Nor would I ever intentionally act contrary to the AFSC Code of Conduct
or Lending Policy Manual.  It was my understanding that the land assessment
information I gave [the customer], which was neither up-to-date nor a formal
opinion as to value, was not subject to [my superior’s] directive or AFSC’s rules.

It bears noting that I did not try to
conceal the fact that I gave land assessment information to [the customer].
Believing my actions to be professionally and ethically permissible, I noted
them in writing on the client’s file for all to see. There was nothing
deceitful about what I did.  In fact, if I hadn’t noted my actions on the file,
nobody would have been aware of the issue.

[
41
]

There is no evidence of any prior history of
disobedience or related performance defaults presented in support of the dismissal
for cause.

[
42
]

There is no suggestion that Ms. Beaudoin had
anything to gain by providing the information she did to the customer.

Analysis

[
43
]

Although Ms. Beaudoin was questioned under Part
5 of the
Alberta Rules of Court
, as well as cross-examined on her
affidavit sworn in support of this application, she was not examined or cross-examined
on the evidence of her belief that she did nothing wrong.  That evidence
remains unchallenged.  AFSC argues the case on the basis that she must have
known because of the emails in June addressing the release of appraisal
information.

[
44
]

Given this evidence, the case must be decided on
the basis that if AFSC had provided her with an opportunity to respond to the
assertion that she had breached the Code of Conduct and Lending Policy Manual,
she would have given the response that we now find in her affidavit.   AFSC has
no proper complaint that the explanation was not given until after the lawsuit
was started. As a matter of good human resources practice as well AFSC’s own
Code of Conduct, the employer should have performed an appropriate
investigation before dismissing her for cause.  A basic aspect of that
investigation would have been to give her an opportunity to explain what had
been discovered.  The only opportunity she was given before she was dismissed
was when she was sent an email by Mr. Thompson asking to explain what she had
done in June.  However, that explanation was given in response to questions
asked of her in mid-November, three months after she released the information, without
a clear understanding what the concern was, and without any indication that her
job was in jeopardy.

[
45
]

The burden of proving that it had just cause to
dismiss summarily lies on the employer:
Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy
,

2015 ABQB 731
,
Elgert v. Home Hardware Stores Limited
,
2010 ABQB
40
,
Gillman v Saan Stores Ltd
,
1992 CanLII 6202 (AB QB)
, 1992
CanLII 6202 (ABQB),
Chettleborough v Canadian Concrete Products Ltd
,

1988 CanLII 3806 (AB QB)
, 1988 CanLII 3806 (ABQB);
Milsom v Corporate
Computers Inc
,
2002 ABQB 948
; and
Chapell v Canadian Pacific
Railway Company
,
2010 ABQB 441
.

[
46
]

There are ten elements that are required for
insubordination to constitute just cause for dismissal, as set out in
Karmel
,
at para.
16
, citing
Wilson v KP Manufacturers (Calgary) Ltd
,
1998 CanLII 18141 (AB QB)
, 1998
225 AR 205, 60 Alta LR (3d) 333 at paras
10-11
and Levitt,
The Law of
Dismissal in Canada
, 2d ed. (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 1992):

1.

the order must be either clear and specific or
must be a breach of policies and procedures well known by the employee;

2.

the order must be within the scope of the
employee’s job duties;

3.

the order must be reasonable and lawful;

4.

the disobedience must be both deliberate and
intentional rather than resulting from an honest mistake as to whether the
order was still in effect or under the reasonable belief that he was not
contravening orders;

5.

the order must involve some matter of
importance;

6.

unless the act of disobedience is particularly
serious it has to be repeated, rather than be an isolated act of disobedience,
in order to constitute cause;

7.

it must be shown that as a result of the
disobedience the relationship was so damaged that it could not be carried
on;

8.

it must be shown that the employee understood or
should have understood that he ran the risk of being terminated for
disregarding the order;

9.

if there is a reasonable explanation for the
disobedience it will not be cause for discharge; and

10.

there will be more latitude shown to long-service employees.

[
47
]

In
Karmel
, Justice Macleod quoted
from
Panton v Everywoman’s Health Centre
(1988)
,
2000 BCCA 621
as
to the level of disobedience required:

In order for wilful disobedience to be just
cause for termination, the employee’s behaviour must be “seriously incompatible
with the employee’s duties… conduct which goes to the root of the contract and
fundamentally strikes at the employment relationship”.

[
48
]

Here, Ms. Beaudoin argues that items 4, 5, 7 and
8 have not been satisfied.  She argues that her disobedience was not deliberate
and intentional, there was no actual adverse consequence of her error, there
was no effort to discuss it with her and consider performance management, and
there was no indication (even in the June emails that AFSC relies on as the
direction) that she was told that dismissal was a possible result.  The
possible consequence of dismissal could only be gleaned from a careful review
of the Code of Conduct, which, of course, deals in general terms and says only
that a breach of any of its terms may lead to termination.

The Disobedience Must be both
Deliberate and Intentional

[
49
]

A review of the email exchange indicates that
although it was clear that Ms. Beaudoin’s superiors believed that they were
instructing her clearly not to release appraisal information, the nature of the
question, as originally posed, seemed to be focused on whether she could give
her opinion as to value, not factual information located in the file.

[
50
]

The Lending Policy Manual is clear that
appraisals “must not be given to customers”.  However, the emails did not
specifically address to her attention to that passage in the manual, nor was
there any indication that there would be any repercussions.

[
51
]

In the circumstance it seems clear that her
explanation, although wrong, was not clearly unreasonable.  Her email enquiry
addressed her opinion of value in respect of the daughter and son-in-law’s
company’s lands.  What she provided about two months later, in August, was
information about the mother’s own lands, and it appears to have been by then
slightly historical.

[
52
]

As I read the emails, although it is clear upon reflection
that the direction was intended to be broad – not to give out appraisal
information – the discussion was understood differently by Ms. Beaudoin.  If I read
the emails the way Ms. Beaudoin says she understood them, when I consider her
later explanation, everything makes sense.

[
53
]

Apart from that email direction, it would have
required some review by her of the policy manual in order to determine the
extent of the direction that management was giving her.

[
54
]

Furthermore, she was transparent about what she
did: she made a note for the file.  She had nothing to gain by doing something
that was requested by the customer.   Her actions do not appear to be an
intentional violation of instruction.  Her memo to file suggests that she
clearly thought she was allowed to do what she did.  She says she was
“assisting a valuable client with a difficult problem within the bounds of my
professional mandate and AFSC’s rules.”

[
55
]

In hindsight, she should have, in light of the
email exchange in June, asked the question specifically in August as to what
she might provide, if anything.

[
56
]

This takes us to the basic question, which is
whether this error, made in these circumstances, amounted to just cause for
summary dismissal of Ms. Beaudoin from a 15-year employment relationship.

[
57
]

In my view, it did not.  A proper investigation
following AFSC’s own Code of Conduct, allowing her to explain, would have
disclosed the disconnect.  It would have resulted in an excellent opportunity
to clarify her duties in her position, which she had held only for about a
year-and-a-half at the time the error was made, and to explain the importance
of why an employee should not disclose to a client even historical appraisal
information on a client’s own property.

[
58
]

Accordingly, I do not accept that her disobedience
has been shown to be both deliberate and intentional.

The Order Must Involve Some
Matter of Importance

[
59
]

Although from AFSC’s perspective it is important
not to give out appraisal information, to avoid possible reliance on it and set
up the corporation for a claim for negligent misstatement, the circumstance
here was that the mother was looking for information on her own lands to allow
some understanding of the property owned by her daughter’s company – different
property, different owner, slightly different time, and far less likelihood of
any repercussion to AFSC.  The facts as understood by Ms. Beaudoin were that
the customer could not have directly relied on the information to come to an
understanding of the value of the land that was in contest.

[
60
]

I accept that this is a subtle distinction that
does not translate well into directions set out in a general policy, and
accordingly Ms. Beaudoin must be seen to have violated the Lending Policy
Manual.  However, it is a factor that weighs in her favour in considering her
explanation.  From her perspective, not only was this breach of minor
importance, the context would have allowed her to believe that she was not
directly contravening what she had been instructed following her initial
inquiry.

It Must Be Shown That the
Employee Understood or Should Have Understood That She Ran the Risk of Being
Terminated for Disregarding the Order

[
61
]

As to item number 8 in the
Karmel

list, nowhere in the email string is there any indication that Ms. Beaudoin was
told that if she gave out appraisal information her job would be in jeopardy.
She could have understood that only from a careful reading of the Lending
Policy Manual
and
the Code of Conduct and Ethics policy.  The direction
in the Code of Conduct is not to “sell, trade, market or distribute any such
product”, and it would be a fair reading of that prohibition to conclude that
she did none of those things.

[
62
]

In the circumstances, AFSC has not met the
burden of proving that there was just cause to dismiss.

Damages

Reasonable Notice

[
63
]

It is clearly correct that Ms. Beaudoin was not
in a “senior management” position. However, given the widely spread-out offices
of AFSC, and the fact that she had been promoted from an “administrative
support” position in 2014, considering herself to have been in a lower “management”
position is not clearly wrong.  That seems to fairly describe her position and
responsibilities.  Her supervisor was in Drumheller, about 75 km away. She must
have had some level of autonomy in carrying out her duties.

[
64
]

The case law on what amount of notice to dismiss
would have been reasonable is fact specific.  Both plaintiff and defendant
cited numerous cases as examples.

[
65
]

The assessment of “reasonable notice” is
premised on the concept, not usually followed in practice, that the employee
should actually have been given reasonable notice of termination and an
opportunity to find another job.  In the circumstances that we have here, if
that were done, it would have been under the cloud of an assertion by the
employer that it had “just cause” for summary dismissal, in a small town.  That
militates in favour of a higher assessment of reasonable notice within might
otherwise be the appropriate range.  She could not have obtained a favourable
letter of reference from AFSC, and any employer asking for a reference from the
Human Resources Department would not have received a favourable comment, given
the circumstances of Ms. Beaudoin’s termination.  It would have been an implied
term of her contract of employment that she not be dismissed for cause when
there was not cause.

[
66
]

In my view, the reasonable period of notice for
a 54-year-old employee of 15 years’ service, with Ms. Beaudoin’s level of
seniority within the organization, given the circumstances here, was 14
months.  She had been with the corporation for a long time.  She was not at the
beginning of her career, and the geographic nature of AFSC’s operations would
have meant that she would have some autonomy.

Mitigation

[
67
]

The assertion of “just cause” creates a further
risk for the employer that we see manifested here: the employee descends into
some level of depression and stress and finds it difficult to look for, or even
accept, alternative work, and by the time she is able to look for work she is
unable to find any in such a small community.

[
68
]

On the one hand, Ms. Beaudoin was “offered” a
job with another financial institution within a month of being dismissed from
AFSC.   AFSC asserts that she should have taken that job, and by failing to
take it she failed to mitigate her claim for damages.  On the other, Ms.
Beaudoin says that she was not then in a state of mind to pursue it.

[
69
]

There is clearly some merit to AFSC’s argument,
but the difficulty is that the offer came too soon following a sudden dismissal
for cause.  Ms. Beaudoin’s response is, in my view, very realistic - even
though there is no evidence of any particular medical treatment or medication
sought or taken in the month or months following her dismissal.   She gave
evidence that she was already on depression medication.  If she were seeking
additional damages for the manner of dismissal (which she is, and which I
discuss below), and if she were asserting a psychological or physiological
consequence in that context, I would expect to see clear evidence of medical
treatment or counselling.  Here, she did not even make use of the EFAP
program.

[
70
]

However, her explanation is nonetheless a
reasonable one for not taking a similar job right away.  This approach is
consistent with the approach in
Lee v 1554478 Ontario Inc
,
2008
CanLII 55467
at para.
14
, where the Court accepted that the employee was not
capable of starting a job search for about four months in circumstances where,
although the employee was not formally dismissed for cause (or at least counsel
did not try to argue that defence), the termination was performance-related.

[
71
]

No doubt some time later Ms. Beaudoin wished she
had pursued the opportunity presented to her so soon after her termination.

[
72
]

The burden of proving that a dismissed employee
has failed to take reasonable steps in mitigation of damages lies upon the
employer.  The employer has provided no evidence of any other jobs that were
available for which she might have applied, but did not, and it rests its case
entirely on the failure to pursue the position with the Chinook Credit Union
and the assertion that Ms. Beaudoin almost entirely focused her efforts on a
“management” position (excepting one administrative position that she did
pursue).

[
73
]

As I have already alluded, I do not fault her
for looking for a “management” position.  There are many levels of
“management”.  He job with AFSC appears to have been one that had some
“management” aspect to it.  She seemed to have some independent responsibility
for appraising land and making loan decisions, at least at first instance, and
having direct interaction with customers while working in a remote location
from her direct supervisor.

[
74
]

There is no evidence that there were any jobs
that she might have applied for but did not, other than the one with Chinook
Credit Union.

Punitive and Aggravated Damages

[
75
]

Ms. Beaudoin claims punitive damages.  Punitive
damages are intended to be just that – punitive:
Whiten v Pilot Insurance
Co
,
2002 SCC 18
, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 595, at para.
36
:

Punitive damages are awarded against a
defendant in exceptional cases for “malicious, oppressive and high-handed”
misconduct that “offends the court’s sense of decency”:
Hill v. Church of
Scientology of Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130, at  para.
196
.  The test thus
limits the award to misconduct that represents a marked departure from ordinary
standards of decent behaviour.  Because their objective is to punish the
defendant rather than compensate a plaintiff (whose just compensation will
already have been assessed), punitive damages straddle the frontier between
civil law (compensation) and criminal law (punishment).

[
76
]

Ms. Beaudoin asserts that the message must be
sent to AFSC so that it does not deal with other employees the same way. The
difficulty with this approach is that it assumes that management of AFSC knew, or
should have known, at the time of termination, that it was seriously off-base
in dismissing Ms. Beaudoin for cause.  The evidence does not support that.

[
77
]

The error that it made, in my view, is a common
one: it acted too soon, without giving the employee an opportunity to explain
her actions.  Conclusions were reached without reaching the final stage of the
investigation - asking for an explanation.  Had management received her
explanation, which is to the effect that she did not realize she was doing
anything wrong, the assertion that it had lost all faith in her would likely
not have been made.  It would have been appropriate to have a candid discussion
with her about her job, responsibilities, and the importance of the appraisals,
particularly given that the Lenders who do appraisals for AFSC are not independently
qualified appraisers.  After 15 years of service, but only a year-and-a-half in
this position, a different response than dismissal would have been appropriate.
(And that is item number 10 in the
Karmel
list.)

[
78
]

The irony here is that Ms. Beaudoin lost her job
for not following company policy, and the employer has failed in its defence of
“just cause” for not following company policy.  Employees cannot be expected to
work to a standard of perfection; neither can the Court expect employers to do
so.

[
79
]

This is not an appropriate case for punitive
damages.

[
80
]

Neither is it an appropriate case for aggravated
damages, for similar reasons.  Aggravated damages in wrongful dismissal claims
are generally awarded because of the manner of dismissal, where the employer’s
conduct was unfair or bad faith, or the conduct was “untruthful, misleading or
unduly insensitive”:
Honda Canada Inc v Keays
,
2008 SCC 39
,
[2009] 2 S.C.R. 362 at para.
57
and
Wallace v United Grain Growers Ltd
,

1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 701, 152 D.L.R. (4
th
) 1 at para.
98
.  Some examples
of the sort of conduct that will trigger aggravated damages are listed in
Merrill
Lynch Canada v Soost
,
2010 ABCA 251
at para.
16
.

[
81
]

As mentioned above, Ms. Beaudoin has tendered no
evidence to show that she suffered any special psychological or physiological
damage from unfair treatment.  She was given the continued opportunity to
access the EFAP coverage.

[
82
]

Not every failed “just cause” defence will
trigger aggravated damages.  In my view, the consequence of a failed “just
cause” defence will simply mean an award at the higher end of what might
otherwise be an appropriate range.  An employer that may have damaged a former
employee’s self-confidence and community reputation cannot complain that the
former employee is allowed a little longer to get back on her feet.

Conclusion

[
83
]

In the result, damages are awarded based on Ms.
Beaudoin’s annual salary, divided by 12 and multiplied by 14.  As mentioned at
the outset, there is no claim for the value of lost benefits.

[
84
]

Pre-judgment interest is awarded, calculated
from the mid-point of the 14-month period, following the approach described in
Christianson
v North
Hill
News Inc
,
1993 ABCA 232
at para.
26
.

[
85
]

Costs would normally be awarded to Ms. Beaudoin
under Schedule “C”, but there may be special factors to consider.  If counsel
are unable to agree on costs, they may contact the masters’ chambers clerk to
arrange to speak to the Court.
